TRAVEL REIMBURSEMENT MANUAL — revision 7
1. Purpose and order of authority. This manual governs employee travel reimbursements submitted from 1 April 2026. Defined terms in section 2 apply everywhere, including appendices. If a case-specific written pre-approval conflicts with the standard limits, the pre-approval controls only where section 6 permits it. Amendment A at the end was adopted later than all numbered sections and controls any inconsistency.

2. Definitions. A "travel day" is a calendar day on which the employee is away from the home work location at midnight, except the departure day is also a travel day even when departure is after midnight local time due to a delayed carrier. A "provided meal" is food included without separately stated cost in lodging, conference registration, or carrier service; dietary unsuitability does not stop it being provided unless the accessibility office documented the restriction before travel. "Remote-site travel" means the destination is more than 80 road kilometers from both the employee's home and assigned office. "Timely" means received in the expense portal within 20 business days after the final travel day. Business days exclude weekends and the company closure dates listed in section 9.

3. Meal allowance. The standard allowance is 68 credits per full travel day. Departure and return days receive 75 percent. Deduct 20 percent for a provided breakfast, 30 percent for lunch, and 50 percent for dinner; percentages are of the unadjusted 68-credit daily allowance. The daily result cannot be below zero. Receipts neither increase nor decrease this allowance.

4. Lodging. Lodging is reimbursable up to 190 credits per night. Taxes stated separately are outside that cap. A conference hotel may be reimbursed up to 240 credits only when the booking was made before the conference block closed and the conference organizer named that hotel. Personal upgrades are never reimbursable.

5. Ground transport. Rail is preferred. A taxi over 55 credits requires either a transit-disruption record or remote-site travel. A manager's convenience statement is not a disruption record.

6. Pre-approval. A director may pre-approve lodging above the standard cap or taxi use without a disruption. The writing must identify the trip and a maximum amount. Pre-approval cannot waive timeliness, turn a personal upgrade into business expense, alter meal deductions, or override a later amendment.

7. Late claims. Finance must reject an untimely claim unless the portal was unavailable for at least four continuous hours on the submission deadline and the employee submitted by noon on the next business day. Manager absence, missing receipts, workload, or an email sent outside the portal does not extend the period.

8. Case file. Mira traveled to Quarry Point, 112 road kilometers from her home but 34 road kilometers from her assigned office. She departed Monday 6 April 2026, stayed away Monday and Tuesday at midnight, and returned Wednesday 8 April. Her director pre-approved "up to 230 credits nightly at the Summit Conference Hotel and taxis up to 90 credits for the Quarry Point trip." The organizer named Summit and the block was still open when she booked at 225 credits nightly. Tuesday conference registration included breakfast. The accessibility office had documented before travel that the provided breakfast could not meet her medically required diet. A Tuesday taxi cost 82 credits; transit operated normally. Mira entered the complete claim in the portal on Monday 11 May. The portal was available throughout. Company closures in this interval were Friday 10 April and Friday 1 May.

9. Calendar note. The weekend days and the two stated closure Fridays are not business days. All other Mondays through Fridays in the interval are business days.

AMENDMENT A — adopted 15 March 2026, effective for travel beginning on or after 1 April 2026. Despite section 6, director pre-approval cannot raise the lodging cap at a named conference hotel while its conference block remains open. Such lodging is capped at the ordinary 190 credits plus separately stated taxes. The amendment does not change taxi authority or the definition of remote-site travel.

DATA ACCESS STANDARD — 2026 consolidated edition
Article 1 — Scope. This standard applies to exports from Atlas, a system containing customer contact, billing, and service telemetry. The decision is made under the version in force when access begins, except a later emergency directive expressly made immediately applicable controls ongoing access.

Article 2 — Definitions. "Direct identifier" includes name, full address, email, telephone number, account number, or any stable value that another company can use to single out a person. A hash is still a direct identifier when it is stable across exports. "Aggregate" means every released cell combines at least 25 distinct customers after all filters. "Internal research" is work performed only by employees on company-managed devices, with no external recipient or publication. A contractor is external even if issued a company email address. "Short access" lasts no more than 30 consecutive days.

Article 3 — Baseline routes. Aggregate, non-identifying data may be approved by the analytics owner. Row-level telemetry without direct identifiers requires privacy review. Any direct identifier normally requires both privacy and security review, a recorded purpose, and deletion date. Marketing consent is irrelevant to security review.

Article 4 — Academic collaboration route. A university collaborator may receive row-level telemetry stripped of direct identifiers if a data-use agreement is executed before access, the ethics approval is current, and privacy approves the transformation. The analytics owner cannot substitute for privacy. No direct identifiers may use this route.

Article 5 — Incident route. During a declared severity-one incident, the incident commander may grant engineers short access to the minimum necessary row-level data. Direct identifiers remain prohibited unless the security duty officer separately approves them. Incident access expires when the incident closes, even if 30 days have not elapsed.

Article 6 — Renewals. Renewal is a new access decision. Prior review can be relied on only if recipients, fields, purpose, environment, and transformation are unchanged. Adding a field or recipient requires the corresponding current route.

Article 7 — Case file. Aster University and the company's employee researcher plan a service-reliability study. The university agreement was signed 2 February 2026 and ethics approval runs through December. Privacy approved an export containing event time rounded to the hour, coarse three-digit postal area, device family, failure code, and `cohort_token`, described in the request as SHA-256(account_number + a secret held by the company). The same token would appear for the same account in every monthly export so longitudinal behavior can be joined. Security was copied on the request but gave no approval. The analytics owner approved it. Access is requested for 24 days. There is no declared incident. The employee says the token is anonymous because the university lacks the secret. Minimum cell size in the planned paper is 40, but the university will receive individual rows. No prior export exists.

Article 8 — Interpretation examples. A randomly regenerated token that changes independently in every export and cannot be linked by the recipient is not stable, though privacy review may still be needed for row-level data. Rounding timestamps does not make individual rows aggregate. Publication cell thresholds govern publication, not the underlying transfer.

EMERGENCY DIRECTIVE 3, issued 20 January 2026. Until withdrawn, stable hashed account values are expressly treated as direct identifiers even if the receiving party cannot reverse the hash or lacks the salt. This clarification applies immediately to new and ongoing access. Academic collaboration may not receive such values. Removal or independently randomized replacement requires a new privacy confirmation.

Exact duplicates are each responsive when stored in separate systems unless the hold notice permits deduplication. "Derived analytics" are records produced from source data; they are not source records. "Verified deletion" means deletion from active systems and expiration from ordinary backups under the stated schedule, with a logged confirmation. Cryptographic erasure counts only if the relevant keys exclusively protect the named records.

3. Customer requests. A verified identity request is due within 30 calendar days. Data needed for contract performance may be retained while necessary. Data under legal hold is retained even after the ordinary purpose ends, and the customer receives the standard limitation notice. Non-held data in the same account remains subject to deletion.

COMMUNITY GRANT AWARD RULEBOOK
Part 1 — Purpose and precedence. The program awards small implementation grants. Eligibility gates are applied before scoring; an ineligible application cannot win regardless of score. The board resolution at the end postdates this edition and overrides conflicting provisions.

Part 2 — Entities. An eligible lead must be a registered nonprofit or a municipal department. An unincorporated group may participate but cannot lead or receive funds. A fiscal sponsor counts as lead only if it signs the application before the deadline and accepts financial responsibility. Two entities under common control count as one applicant for the one-award limit.

Part 3 — Timing. Applications are due 17:00 local program time on 30 June. Portal receipts control. A submission may be cured within two business days only for a missing attachment that existed before the deadline; signatures, budgets, and partner commitments cannot be created during cure. A portal outage extension requires an official outage of at least 30 continuous minutes during the final two hours.

Part 4 — Budget. Requests must be 20,000 through 80,000 credits inclusive. At least 70 percent must be implementation cost. Administrative cost is any general management, accounting, rent, or fundraising amount. Equipment used directly to deliver the project is implementation. Contingency is administrative unless allocated to named implementation tasks.

Part 5 — Conflicts. A reviewer with a financial relationship to any applicant or named delivery partner must recuse. Mere residence in the served municipality is not a conflict. A recused reviewer's score is discarded, not averaged as zero.

Part 6 — Scoring. Eligible applications receive impact up to 40, feasibility up to 30, equity up to 20, and evidence up to 10. Normally the highest total wins. A proposal below 18 on feasibility cannot win. Ties are broken by higher equity, then lower requested amount.
